sentences.text: Alwalkeria is an extinct avemetatarsalian genus known from the Late Triassic Lower Maleri Formation of India, estimated to reach about one meter in length.
The partial skull measures approximately 4 centimeters in length, though some estimates suggest the animal may have reached only 50 centimeters in total length.
Gregory S. Paul estimated a weight of 2 kilograms and a length of 1.5 meters in 2010.
Alwalkeria possessed heterodont dentition in the upper jaw, with teeth varying in shape based on their position, featuring thin, straight front teeth and backward-curving side teeth.
This dental arrangement suggests Alwalkeria was an omnivore with a varied diet including insects, small vertebrates, and plants.
Alwalkeria is unique among basal dinosaurs for its teeth without denticles and a proportionally wider mandibular symphysis than almost any other known dinosaur.
The animal also possessed a very large articulation between the perone and the ankle.
The genus Alwalkeria was first described by Sankar Chatterjee in 1987 as a basal theropod.
The original name Walkeria was rejected because it was preoccupied by a bryozoan.
In 1987, Chatterjee named Walkeria maleriensis based on specimen ISI R 306, containing a partial skull, around 28 vertebrae, femur fragments, and an astragalus.
In 2005, Rauhut and Remes found Alwalkeria to be a chimera with a crurotarsan skull and dinosaurian femur and astragalus.
There is one recorded fossil occurrence of Alwalkeria in the Paleobiology Database.
The fossil remains may belong to a juvenile individual, consisting of anterior jaw fragments, 28 incomplete vertebrae, most of a femur, an astragalus, and a partial skull.

Subsequent work recognized the chimeric status of the fossils, indicating they belong to multiple unrelated taxa, where some bones may belong to a dinosaur while the skull is likely from a pseudosuchian.
Researchers identified the distal femur as an indeterminate representative of the pseudosuchian clade.
Alwalkeria is classified within the superorder Dinosauria and the order Saurischia, with the current scientific consensus placing it at a basal position within Saurischia.

McDavid, Marchant, and Reid in 2026 revised the nomenclature of Alickmeron maleriensis, considering it a junior objective synonym of Alwalkeria maleriensis and reinterpreting it as an indeterminate member of Pan-Aves.
Alwalkeria lived during the Late Triassic in the Lower Maleri Formation of India, with fossils dating to the Carnian stage of the Triassic, approximately 235 to 228 million years ago.
Alwalkeria lived at the end of the Triassic, approximately 220 million years ago, during the Carnian stage in what is now the Indian subcontinent.
Alwalkeria lived during the Carnian stage, from 237 to 227.3 million years ago.
It is debated whether Alwalkeria belongs to a podokesaurid theropod, a herrerasaur, or an Eoraptor-like basal eusaurischian dinosaur, and specifically whether it is a theropod or a basal saurischian.
It is debated whether the skull material belongs to a dinosaur or a crocodylomorph.
It is debated whether the femora belong to a novel lagerpetid named Alickmeron maleriensis or to Alwalkeria.
It is debated whether Alwalkeria should be assigned to Pan-Aves incertae sedis or to the lagerpetid clade.
Rauhut and Remes in 2005 hypothesized that Alwalkeria was a chimera, with the anterior skull part belonging to a crurotarsian and the vertebrae belonging to other ancient reptiles.
